vignette:
Marianne was seventy-nine when she first came for help, a widowed European American tailor who had spent most of her adult life working with her hands in a small alteration shop and, more recently, from a worktable set up in a bright spare room in her home. She spoke softly and with care, but there were moments when her face tightened and her jaw set as if she were bracing against something only she could see. The event she had lived through during military service remained difficult for her to tell in any orderly way. When she tried, the pieces did not sit together properly. She could give fragments - the sense of urgency, the sight of blood, the awful fear in the air - but she could not place the moments in the right order, and when she reached for the details she often stopped and said that it was "all mixed up." She also said she had never been able to put the frightening event into words. It was not simply that she disliked talking about it; the memory seemed to arrive in her body before it became language, and when it surfaced she felt a surge of rage that startled her. She would sometimes clench her hands in her lap and say that what happened was "unforgivable," her eyes bright with anger that seemed to come as soon as she remembered.

Marianne described how the event had involved military violence and blood, and that those two things still carried a particular force for her now. At times an unwanted thought would strike her out of nowhere - while threading a needle, folding fabric, or sitting quietly at her kitchen table - and she would be pulled back to that time without wanting to go there. Certain conversation topics had the same effect. If someone mentioned the military, wartime injuries, or even stories about old conflicts on the television or radio, she would become visibly tense and try to steer the discussion away. She was not able to tolerate the sight of blood in any form; even a small cut on her finger, a blood pressure cuff leaving a faint mark, or a scene on television was enough to make her look away and feel flooded with the same alarm she associated with the original event. She said she knew these reactions were excessive in the present, but in the moment they felt immediate and real, as if the past had broken in without warning.

Over the years, Marianne had gradually narrowed her world. After her husband died, she found that she was increasingly reluctant to see friends, even those who had known her for decades. Invitations to lunch, church gatherings, and neighborhood visits often went unanswered. She would tell herself that she was tired or busy with sewing orders, but privately she had come to dread the effort of appearing unchanged when she felt so altered inside. She also found herself avoiding situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful. If a neighbor praised her work and suggested she should be proud, or if one of her nieces spoke warmly about future plans, she would feel an urge to shut the feeling down before it could take hold. Positive emotions felt unsafe to her, as if allowing herself to hope would only set her up to be hurt again. She had come to believe that nothing good could happen to her anymore. "I used to be a happy person," she said, with a tired, flat certainty, "but now I'm always miserable." She repeated that she felt dead inside, as though the life that once came naturally to her had been hollowed out.

This sense of emptiness showed in the way she lived. In her tailoring room, which should have been a place of comfort and mastery, she often worked alone for long stretches, turning down social calls so she would not have to explain herself or risk being drawn into cheerful conversation. Friends gradually stopped asking as often, and she noticed their distance with a kind of resigned sadness. She did not describe herself as lonely so much as sealed off. Even on days when the work went well, she was careful not to let herself settle into contentment. She would finish a hem, hear a kind comment from a customer, and then immediately push away the pleasant feeling, telling herself it could not last. What frightened her most was not any single memory, but the conviction that there was no future in which she could return to the person she had been. By the time she sought help, it was not because the memories had changed, but because the isolation had become harder to bear and she was beginning to fear that her remaining years would be spent cut off from others, from happiness, and from any sense that life could still offer something good.
